text: Right now, by one scientist's estimate, your brain could hold about a plastic spoon's worth of plastic.
That estimate comes from a 2025 study that analysed brain tissue from people who had died, and reported far more tiny plastic than anyone expected.
They found it in blood. In the arteries of patients who then had more heart attacks and strokes. In the water you drink.
And the plastic industry is accused of knowing, for decades, that recycling would never solve the problem. It denies that.
But there's a twist. A growing number of scientists now say some of these terrifying numbers might be wrong. And that could be even worse.
To understand how plastic got inside you, start with how much of it there is.
In twenty years, the world doubled its plastic production, to around four hundred and sixty million tonnes a year.
And only about nine percent of all that plastic waste actually gets recycled. The rest is burned, buried, or dumped.
Here's the problem. Plastic doesn't really go away. It just gets smaller.
Sun, waves and heat break it into microplastics, smaller than a grain of rice, and then into nanoplastics, far thinner than a human hair.
Small enough to slip into places plastic was never supposed to go.
And it isn't only bottles. Every time you drive, your tyres shed plastic dust onto the road. Every time you wash a fleece, it sheds tiny fibres.
One 2017 estimate found that washing synthetic clothes and wearing down tyres cause almost two thirds of the plastic that reaches the ocean already as tiny particles.
In 2024, one study looked at bottled water with a powerful new microscope technique.
It found an average of about two hundred and forty thousand plastic particles in a single litre. Most of them were nanoplastics.
And it doesn't stay in the bottle.
In 2022, researchers in Amsterdam tested the blood of twenty two healthy adults.
Seventeen of them had plastic in their blood.
Then doctors in Italy looked inside the clogged neck arteries of patients having surgery.
Most of the plaques had micro or nanoplastics in them. And over the next three years, those patients were about four and a half times more likely to have a heart attack, a stroke, or die.
The study couldn't prove the plastic caused it. But it set off alarm bells around the world.
It's even turned up in the placenta, the organ that feeds a baby before it's born. A small Italian study found plastic in four of the six placentas it tested.
And then, the brain.
The 2025 study compared brains from people who died in 2016 with brains from people who died in 2024.
The newer brains held about fifty percent more plastic. Brains had far more than livers or kidneys. And the brains of people with dementia had even more.
Again, that doesn't prove plastic causes dementia. A damaged brain might simply be worse at clearing it out.
But if plastic is everywhere, inside everyone, somebody had to let it get this far.
For decades, you were told the answer was simple. Rinse it. Sort it. Recycle it.

An NPR investigation found industry documents from as far back as the 1970s doubting that plastic recycling could ever pay off on a large scale. The industry says it never intentionally misled anyone.
In 2024, California's attorney general sued ExxonMobil, one of the world's biggest plastic producers, accusing it of deceiving the public about recycling for decades.
Exxon denies it, and says its advanced recycling works. The case isn't over.
And production isn't slowing down. Without new rules, the OECD projects the world could use almost three times as much plastic by 2060, with less than a fifth of the waste recycled.
But just as public fear reached its peak, the science itself started to crack.
Here's how many of these studies measured plastic. They heat a tissue sample until it breaks apart, then read the chemical fragments, like a fingerprint.
The problem? Some fragments from ordinary body fat look a lot like fragments from plastic.
Take out the water, and the brain is about sixty percent fat.
In other words, some of that plastic... might not be plastic at all.

One analysis listed eighteen studies that didn't properly account for these false positives. Scientists have now formally challenged at least seven high-profile papers, including the brain study, the artery study and the bottled water study.
Some critics even suggest that rising obesity, more fat in the body, could explain part of the jump in brain plastic.
The original researchers push back. They say the critics are speculating without data of their own, though they admit their methods can still be improved.
One of the scientists behind the blood study says she's still convinced the plastic is there. But the true amount could be half what they measured, or ten times more.
Critics say quite a few papers, in the rush to publish, skipped basic lab checks, like running blank samples to catch contamination.
So is the whole microplastics scare just hype? Not so fast.
Even one of the harshest critics says it's safe to assume plastic is inside us. The fight is over how much, and what it's doing.
And in October, a study in Nature found that tiny plastic in water isn't as harmless as we thought. Its surface can produce aggressive molecules that can damage cells.
That was in the lab, not in people. But it's a possible way plastic could do real damage inside the body.
And plastic rarely travels alone. Many plastics contain added chemicals, like BPA and phthalates, which pediatricians warn can interfere with hormones.

Governments are starting to move. The EPA has, for the first time, proposed adding microplastics to its list of drinking water contaminants it may one day regulate. And the U.S. health department is spending a hundred and forty four million dollars to study the risks.
Meanwhile, some clinics already charge thousands to clean plastic out of your blood, before anyone knows how much is really there.
And the global treaty meant to end plastic pollution is still stuck, with countries split over whether to limit production.
Which leaves you in the strangest possible place.
The scary headlines may have overstated how much plastic is in your brain. And shaky studies could even help the plastic industry wave the whole problem away.
But plastic is almost certainly inside you, it's in the water you drink, and production keeps climbing.
Pediatricians already suggest a few cheap precautions: don't microwave food in plastic when you can avoid it, and keep plastic out of the dishwasher. Heat makes it shed chemicals.
The real question isn't whether there's plastic in you. It's how long we keep making more of it, before we find out what it's doing.
So be honest: are you checking your water bottle right now?
